summary: The note is a Wikipedia article on the availability heuristic, a mental shortcut where judgments of frequency, likelihood or importance are based on how easily examples come to mind. It traces the concept's origin in Tversky and Kahneman's 1973 work, reviews key experiments (the K-word study, famous-name recall, ease-of-retrieval studies, Vaughn's uncertainty study), and surveys applications in media, health, business, education, criminal justice, perceived risk and vividness effects. The article is flagged as needing additional citations for verification.
one_line: A mental shortcut where people judge how likely or frequent something is based on how easily examples come to mind.
key_facts: The availability heuristic, also known as availability bias, is a mental shortcut that relies on immediate examples that come to a given person's mind when evaluating a specific topic, concept, method, or decision.
In 1973, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman first studied this phenomenon and labeled it the "availability heuristic".
In the late 1960s and early 1970s, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman began work on a series of papers examining "heuristic and biases" used in judgment under uncertainty.

In Tversky and Kahneman's first examination of availability heuristics, participants were asked whether a random word from an English text is more likely to start with K or to have K as the third letter.
A typical text contains twice as many words that have "K" as the third letter than "K" as the first letter.
Chapman (1967) described a bias in the judgment of the frequency with which two events co-occur, which led to the labeling of the illusory correlation effect.
In Schwarz and colleagues' study, participants rated themselves as more assertive after recalling six examples of assertive behavior, but less assertive after recalling twelve examples.
Vaughn (1999) found that students used the availability heuristic to predict grades when asked at the beginning of the semester and about their hardest final.
In a 2010 study, people watching vivid violent media gave higher estimates of the prevalence of crime and police immorality in the real world.
Many people think the likelihood of dying from shark attacks is greater than dying from being hit by falling airplane parts, when more people actually die from falling airplane parts.

In a 1992 study, participants read case descriptions of hypothetical patients with symptoms that could have been caused by AIDS, leukemia, influenza, meningitis, or appendicitis; either the more common influenza or the more publicized AIDS was chosen.
Franklin Templeton's annual Global Investor Sentiment Survey found 66 percent of respondents believed the S&P 500 was flat or down in 2009, while the S&P 500 saw 26.5 percent annual returns in 2009.
In Craig R. Fox's course evaluation study, students asked to write ten suggestions rated the course less harshly than students asked to write two suggestions.
In a 1989 study of 312 university students acting as mock jurors, jurors were most influenced by the most recent act, with the witness lying second remembered more than earlier truthful testimony.
